title: Passing through Little Rock
description: 'Passing through Little Rock' is in A Good Journey (Berkeley: Turtle Island Foundation, 1977), Ortiz's second collection; Woven Stone's contents place it at page 98. It is a poem about driving through an American city that has buried the Indian peoples who lived there, and it is the sharpest of his short political lyrics.
plot_or_argument: The poem's argument is made by the collision of two kinds of name. Quapaw and Waccamaw are the peoples of the region through which the speaker is driving - the Quapaw gave Arkansas its name by a chain of French transliterations - and the poem finds them surviving only as words on billboards, which is to say as tourist signage, while the town itself is crummy, ordinary, and indifferent. Ortiz's short flat lines refuse the elegiac register that the material would invite; the anger is in the adjective and in the quotation marks around the tribal names, which mark them as someone else's speech. The turn at the end is not to lament but to a wish for birth - a clean river, a new earth, the noise it makes being born - and the wish is placed beyond the next hill, which means it is not available where the speaker is. That structure, in which the poem's hope is located outside the poem's own landscape, is characteristic of Ortiz's political writing, and it is why the poem can be read both as a critique and as a prayer. Its anger is understated and its formal means are very small: a handful of short lines, one quotation, one wish.
narrative_structure: A short free-verse poem in two movements: the description of the town and its billboard names, then the wish to cross the next hill, ending on the image of the earth being born.
meter_and_prosody: Short unpunctuated lines; flat, deliberate colloquialism ('crummy town'); tribal names in quotation marks; a turn from statement to wish; and an ending in sensory immediacy.
historical_context: A Good Journey appeared in 1977, the year of Silko's Ceremony, and belongs to the decade in which Native American writing entered the American literary mainstream; the poem's occasion is a road trip through the South, and its subject is the relation between the places Native people were removed from and the places they are driven through. Little Rock carries its own history of segregation, which the poem leaves implicit.
literary_significance: The poem is a frequent anthology choice for the political side of Ortiz's work and is one of the three Ortiz selections in the Norton's period. Its record is also one of the two in which the last American dates were settled, from the contents of Woven Stone.
bibliographical_notes: First published in A Good Journey (Berkeley: Turtle Island Foundation, 1977); reprinted in Woven Stone (Tucson: University of Arizona Press, 1992), p. 98. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the erasure of Native peoples from the American landscape and their survival as brand names, which the poem renders as a fact of the roadside. The second is the American town as an ordinary place of forgetting, crummy rather than monstrous. The third is hope figured as geography, since what the speaker wants lies over the next hill. The fourth is naming and history, because the poem's whole charge depends on the reader knowing that the billboard words are the names of nations.
summary: The poem opens with the old Indian ghosts - 'Quapaw', 'Waccamaw' - which are 'just billboard words in this crummy town'. It goes on to describe the speaker passing through Little Rock, Arkansas, and the poem's closing movement is a wish for escape: 'I just want to cross the next hill, / through that clump of trees / and come out on the other side / and see a clean river, / the whole earth new / and hear the noise it makes / at birth.'
critical_context: Kenneth Lincoln's early survey of Ortiz reads the poem within the A Good Journey sequence as one of its encounters with the non-Indian world; critics of the anthology have used it to make the point that the Norton's own annotation of the Quapaw and Waccamaw as tribes of Arizona is wrong, since both are peoples of Arkansas. The error is the anthology's, not the poem's.
research_notes: The poem's date and its place in A Good Journey rest on Woven Stone's contents list; the reading above is of the portions of the text quoted in reviews and criticism, not of a complete transcription.

title: From Sand Creek
description: From Sand Creek (New York: Thunder's Mouth Press, 1981) is Ortiz's best-known book: a sequence that takes the massacre of Cheyenne and Arapaho people at Sand Creek, Colorado, in 1864 and sets it against the condition of Native American veterans in the 1970s, when Ortiz was working with patients at a Veterans Administration hospital. The Norton prints an excerpt, and it is the one book-length work of his in the anthology.
plot_or_argument: From Sand Creek is the book in which Ortiz's two subjects, the survival of Native peoples and the damage done to individual Native men, become one argument. The massacre is presented as documentary - the sequence quotes and paraphrases the record, and in an afterword Ortiz names his sources - and the lyrics around it are what the documentary cannot hold: the boredom of the hospital, the drinking, the ordinary tenderness of a friend, the speaker's sense that the history he is writing down is happening in his own body. The refrains do the structural work, returning the reader to the same few sentences so that they acquire the force of a liturgy, and the effect is closer to a memorial service than to a history. Ortiz has said that the book grew out of his time at the Fort Lyon Veterans Administration Hospital in Colorado, where he came to see the veterans he met as casualties of the same long war, and that intention is what makes the book's politics more than topical: the Sand Creek of 1864 and the Vietnam of the 1970s are treated as one event with two dates. Its formal innovation, which later Native writing has often followed, is the combination of verse and document without hierarchy, so that the archive and the poem are given equal weight and neither is allowed to explain the other.
narrative_structure: A three-part sequence, with lyrics enclosing a prose historical middle section, recurring refrains across the parts, and a typography that leaves space on the page as part of the form; an afterword documents the sources.
meter_and_prosody: Short unpunctuated lyric lines and plain declarative prose; repetition of a small number of sentences as refrains; documentary quotation; no ironic distance; and a flatness of tone that refuses both outrage and consolation.
historical_context: Published in 1981, in a period of renewed Native American political organisation and of public argument about the Vietnam veteran; Ortiz was working at the Fort Lyon VA hospital in Colorado when the book was conceived, and its publication by Thunder's Mouth Press put it in the small press circuit that carried much Native writing of the 1970s and 1980s.
literary_significance: From Sand Creek is the most studied single book by an Acoma writer and one of the central texts of the Native American Renaissance; it won the Pushcart Prize for poetry and is the reason Ortiz is often described as the poet of continuance. The Norton Anthology of American Literature prints an excerpt, and the book is a standard presence on American literature syllabi.
bibliographical_notes: First published as From Sand Creek (New York: Thunder's Mouth Press, 1981); reissued by the University of Arizona Press in 2000. The Norton prints an excerpt. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the Sand Creek massacre itself, recorded as fact and refused as spectacle. The second is the continuity of violence against Indigenous peoples from the nineteenth-century frontier to the twentieth-century war, which the structure of the book asserts by juxtaposition. The third is trauma and testimony, since the veterans of the 1970s speak in the same book as the survivors of 1864. The fourth is survival and continuance, which Ortiz's work never abandons: the book is a memorial, but it is also an argument that the people are still here.
summary: The sequence is in three parts. The first and third are lyrics in Ortiz's short unpunctuated lines, many of them spoken by a veteran or by the poet in the hospital, and they record ordinary American life - the ward, the bus, the town, the television - alongside the aftermaths of the war in Vietnam. The middle part is a prose history of the Sand Creek massacre of 29 November 1864, in which a Colorado volunteer regiment under John Chivington attacked a camp of Cheyenne and Arapaho under Black Kettle, who had been told they were under army protection, and killed some two hundred people, most of them women, children and old men. Across the sequence, lines recur as refrains - 'it is not a story' among them - and the book's spacing and typography put the historical prose and the contemporary lyric on the same page.
critical_context: Criticism reads the book's mixing of genres as its main achievement and its refrains as the device that holds the two histories together; it is usually discussed with Silko's Ceremony and with the documentary poetics of the 1970s. The comparison with Whitman - a long American poem that includes everything - is common and usually qualified by the observation that Ortiz's inclusiveness is forensic rather than celebratory.
research_notes: The sequence was not read in full for this record; the description rests on the published accounts of its structure, its three parts and its refrains. The details of the massacre are given as the book and the standard histories give them.

title: The Drowned Children
description: 'The Drowned Children' is the first poem of Descending Figure (New York: Ecco Press, 1980), Glück's third collection, where it opens the section called 'The Garden'. It is a short unrhymed lyric spoken over the bodies of children who have drowned, and it is one of the poems in which the mythic and the domestic first come together in her work.
plot_or_argument: The poem is a test case for Glück's early manner. It takes the most sentimental subject in nineteenth-century verse - drowned children - and writes about it with a coldness that is deliberately unbearable, refusing both the Victorian consolation and the modern ironising that would be the easy alternative. The effect is produced by two things: the second person, which addresses the dead as though they could hear, and the flatness of the declarative sentences, which do not rise into grief. The poem belongs with the Persephone material that dominates Descending Figure - the daughter taken down into the underworld, the mother left above - and reading it that way makes its refusal of consolation a mythological argument: the descent is real, and the poem will not pretend that the return cancels it. Its brevity matters. Glück's poems of this period are short because she cuts the connective tissue that would explain the emotion, so that the reader is left with the image and the statement and has to supply the grief, which is the effect she spent her career refining.
narrative_structure: A single short lyric in unrhymed free verse, in a series of statements addressed to the dead, with no narrative development and an ending that refuses to close the scene.
meter_and_prosody: Short declarative lines with almost no punctuation; a flat, unemphatic tone; concrete nouns and almost no adjectives of feeling; the second person used as address to the dead; and an absence of simile, so that the poem never converts the bodies into symbols.
historical_context: Descending Figure (1980) was Glück's third book, five years after The House on Marshland, and the one in which she began the sequence of biblical and classical narratives that would structure Ararat, The Wild Iris and Meadowlands. It appeared in the year of her marriage to John Dranow, whose name recurs in the later poems, and it is the book in which the family material of her mature work first becomes explicit.
literary_significance: The poem is the standard introduction to Glück's early manner and one of the poems by which the Descending Figure volume is known; it is a Norton selection. Its presence in the anthology places her 1980 work beside the confessional poetry of the 1960s and the mythic poetry of the 1980s, which is where the criticism usually puts it.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Descending Figure (New York: Ecco Press, 1980), the opening poem of the section 'The Garden'; collected in The First Four Books of Poems (1995) and Poems 1962-2012 (2012). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is death, and specifically the death of children, which the poem treats as an event without compensation. The second is the failure of mourning, since the poem describes a grief that cannot be converted into meaning. The third is the mythological underworld that Descending Figure keeps invoking, which gives the drowned children a genealogy. The fourth is the gaze, since the poem is about looking at something one cannot help, which is also Glück's account of what a lyric does.
summary: The poem addresses the drowned children directly, describing them as lying in the water, and it holds the scene at a distance rather than dramatising it: the water, the light, the bodies, and a speaker who looks at them without being able to intervene. Its tone is flat and its sentences are short, and the poem refuses the consolations - of memory, of mourning, of meaning - that an elegy would normally offer. The children are not named and their parents are not present; what the poem keeps is the fact of the death and the uselessness of looking at it.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem with the Persephone poems of the same volume and treats its coldness as a deliberate refusal of the elegiac tradition; the standard account of Glück's development calls Descending Figure the book in which her mythic method appears. It is less discussed than the title poem, which is the volume's statement.
research_notes: The description rests on the poem's placement in the collection and on the critical accounts of the volume; the text was not transcribed in full for this record.

title: Descending Figure
description: 'Descending Figure' is the title poem of Glück's third collection (New York: Ecco Press, 1980), where it closes the first section after the poems of 'The Garden'. It is the poem that states the volume's governing image - the descent - and it is the one in which the mythological method of her later books is first fully visible.
plot_or_argument: The title poem is where the volume's argument becomes explicit. Glück's earlier books had worked through the family and through the imagery of the garden, and Descending Figure adds the vertical axis: what comes down, and what it costs to come down. The religious vocabulary is present but undoctrinal - the descent is not named as incarnation, and the poem keeps the theological reading available without requiring it - and the poem's power comes from its refusal to say whether the descent is a fall or a gift. That ambiguity is what the later books, and especially The Wild Iris, would build on: in The Wild Iris the divine speaks from the garden and the human answers, and the relation between them is exactly the descent this poem describes without a speaker to receive it. Read as an ars poetica, the poem also states Glück's method: the poem goes down into loss because that is where the material is, and it does not come back up with a consolation.
narrative_structure: A short unrhymed lyric in the title position of its volume, organised as a series of statements about descent in different registers, ending without resolution.
literary_form: Poem (title poem of the collection, unrhymed lyric)
meter_and_prosody: Austere, short-lined free verse; abstract nouns used with concrete force; an almost complete absence of simile; a tone of statement rather than address; and an ending that stops rather than concludes.
historical_context: Descending Figure appeared in 1980 from Ecco Press, the small press that published most of Glück's books and that gave her work its characteristic austere presentation. The volume's mythological and biblical material belongs to the years in which American poetry was turning back to narrative and to myth after the confessional 1960s, and Glück's version of that turn was to keep the first person while emptying it of autobiography.
literary_significance: The poem gives the volume its title and its argument, and it is the clearest short statement of the mythic method that would produce Ararat and The Wild Iris. It is a Norton selection, and the pairing of it with 'The Drowned Children' is how the anthology represents the 1980 book.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Descending Figure (New York: Ecco Press, 1980); collected in The First Four Books of Poems (1995) and Poems 1962-2012 (2012). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is descent itself, in its religious, physical and artistic senses, held together without being reconciled. The second is mortality and the decline of the body, which the poem treats as a fact rather than a tragedy. The third is the sacred, invoked in a vocabulary that refuses to commit to a doctrine. The fourth is the work of art, which the poem presents as a going-down into the material rather than a rising above it.
summary: The poem works the idea of descent as both a physical and a spiritual movement: the figure that comes down, the light that falls, the body that declines. It holds several scales at once - the religious descent of the divine into the world, the aging and deterioration of a body, and the artist's own going-down into the material he or she works with - and it does not settle which is primary. The tone is austere and the sentences are short, and the poem ends without resolving the descent into an ascent.
critical_context: The standard critical account treats the title poem as the volume's thesis and reads it with the Persephone material; the descent is usually glossed as the descent into the underworld that structures the whole book. Later criticism reads it as anticipating the theological sequences of the 1990s.
research_notes: The description rests on the poem's position in the volume and on the critical accounts of it; the text was not transcribed in full for this record.

title: Vespers
description: 'Vespers' is one of the ten evening prayers in The Wild Iris (New York: Ecco Press, 1992), the collection for which Glück won the Pulitzer Prize in 1993; the Norton's selection is the fourth of them, which begins 'I don't wonder where you are anymore'. The book is built on the monastic hours - seven Matins and ten Vespers - and alternates the voices of flowers, a gardener-poet and the divine.
plot_or_argument: The poem is a prayer addressed to a God who has been relocated into a gardener, and its theology is worked out through the difference between two people in the same garden. John has peace as a possession; the speaker has it only as a passage, a light that goes through and is not held. The image the poem ends on - bright light through the bare tree - is exactly the difference it has been describing: the bare tree is not fed by the light, it is only lit by it, and the light leaves. The first line's 'anymore' carries the poem's history in a word: the speaker used to look for God and has stopped, and what replaces the search is not faith but accuracy - she knows where God is, and it is with someone else. Glück's handling of the sequence is what makes the poem more than a domestic vignette: because 'Vespers' is the name of a liturgical hour, the poem is formally an evening prayer, and its complaint is delivered inside the form of devotion, which never breaks. The garden, the trowel, the lettuces and the lilies are literal, and they are also the whole apparatus of the book's theology - creation speaking back to its creator - so that a poem about weeding is a poem about the relation between the human and the divine. It is the most anthologised of the Vespers poems and the one by which the collection is usually taught.
narrative_structure: A single unrhymed lyric in the sequence's Vespers form, moving from a statement of God's location through a description of John's gardening to a closing simile that states the speaker's own condition; roughly sixteen short lines.
meter_and_prosody: Plain declarative sentences in the second person, addressed to God; domestic and horticultural vocabulary held without irony; a single long simile at the end that carries the whole emotional weight; no punctuation of emphasis and no rhetorical heightening.
historical_context: The Wild Iris was written, by Glück's own account, in about ten weeks in the summer of 1992 and published by Ecco that year; it won the Pulitzer Prize in 1993. Its structure follows the monastic hours, and the sequence's theology is worked out across the flowers' speeches, the gardener's prayers and the divine's replies, in a garden on a property in Vermont.
literary_significance: 'Vespers' is the poem by which The Wild Iris is most often represented in anthologies and courses, and the collection is the book on which Glück's Nobel Prize was most often justified. It is a Norton selection and the latest of her three poems in the anthology's period.
bibliographical_notes: First published in The Wild Iris (New York: Ecco Press, 1992); collected in Poems 1962-2012 (2012). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the presence and absence of God, handled not as doubt but as relocation: the divine is in the garden and in another person, not in the speaker's experience. The second is the unequal distribution of peace, which the poem records without self-pity and without explaining. The third is work and attention, since the garden's labour is the poem's medium for contemplation. The fourth is transience, carried by twilight, the first lilies, the bare tree and the light that passes through.
summary: The poem begins by saying that the speaker no longer wonders where God is: 'You're in the garden; you're where John is, / in the dirt, abstracted, holding his green trowel.' It describes John's way of gardening - fifteen minutes of intense effort, fifteen minutes of ecstatic contemplation - and the speaker's relation to it: sometimes she works beside him, weeding and thinning the lettuces, and sometimes she watches from the porch near the upper garden until twilight makes lamps of the first lilies. The poem turns in its last lines: peace never leaves John, but it rushes through the speaker not as sustenance the flower holds but 'like bright light through the bare tree'.
critical_context: Critics read the Vespers poems as the human half of the book's dialogue and treat the sequence as a whole as a modern book of hours; the fourth Vespers is regularly discussed for its simile of light through the bare tree, which is taken as the collection's image of the difference between revelation and possession. The Nobel citation's phrase about austere beauty is usually illustrated from this book.
research_notes: The text of this Vespers was read for this record from a published transcription; the Norton's own page reference was not established, and the anthology may print a different Vespers under the same title, since the book contains ten poems so named. The record identifies the poem by its first line.

title: Borderlands/La Frontera: The New Mestiza
description: Borderlands/La Frontera: The New Mestiza, published by Aunt Lute Books in 1987, is Gloria Anzaldúa's central work and one of the founding texts of Chicana feminism: a book in seven chapters that refuses to be one genre, moving between autobiography, revisionist history, myth, poetry and theory, and between English, Spanish and Nahuatl. The Norton Anthology of American Literature prints two of its chapters, 'La conciencia de la mestiza / Towards a New Consciousness' and 'How to Tame a Wild Tongue', which are its philosophical climax and its most quoted argument about language.
plot_or_argument: The book's argument is cumulative and its method is collision: a passage of autobiography will be followed by a page of pre-Columbian history, then a poem, then a paragraph of theory, without transition, so that the reader is made to experience the border's simultaneity rather than be told about it. Anzaldúa's key moves recur. The first is to treat the border as an internal as well as a geographic fact, so that the queer Chicana who leaves home is both traitor and exile. The second is to identify language with identity: 'Ethnic identity is twin skin to linguistic identity - I am my language', and the taming of the wild tongue in school is therefore a form of violence that the book is written to undo. The third is the refusal of the binary: the mestiza does not choose between the Mexican and the American, the Spanish and the English, the Catholic and the indigenous, but inhabits the crossing and develops a tolerance for contradiction that Anzaldúa calls a new consciousness. The fourth is her insistence that theory is written from a body and a life - from a childhood of fieldwork and sunburn, from diabetes and from the experience of being a lesbian in a culture that condemned it. The prose is deliberately unacademic even when it is doing theory: it addresses the reader as 'you', it breaks into lists and poems, and it leaves Spanish untranslated, which was the point.
narrative_structure: Seven chapters, each mixing prose, poetry and untranslated Spanish, moving from the history and myth of the borderland through the author's own life to the theoretical statement of the final chapters; the Norton prints chapters five and seven, which are the argument's hinge and its conclusion.
literary_form: Genre-crossing book of essays, autobiography, history and poetry
meter_and_prosody: Bilingual and unglossed; long anaphoric sentences broken by poems and lists; direct address to the reader; first person alternating with third; and a polemical register that keeps the idiom of the Valley in the theory.
historical_context: Aunt Lute Books, a San Francisco feminist press, published the book in 1987, and it appeared in the decade in which Chicano studies entered US universities and in which women of colour criticised both white feminism and nationalist Chicano politics. It was preceded by This Bridge Called My Back (1981), which Anzaldúa co-edited with Cherríe Moraga, and it became a set text in women's studies, ethnic studies and queer theory within a few years of publication.
literary_significance: Borderlands/La Frontera is one of the books that changed the American academy's understanding of identity in the late twentieth century; the term 'mestiza consciousness' is now standard in feminist and postcolonial theory, and the book is credited, with Moraga's and Audre Lorde's work, with establishing the category of women of colour. The Norton's printing of two chapters is the anthology's principal representation of Chicana writing, and it takes a work of theory as literature, which is itself the book's argument.
bibliographical_notes: First published by Aunt Lute Books (San Francisco) in 1987; a second edition followed in 1999 and a fourth, with a new preface, in 2012. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject, and the book's whole occasion, is the border as a lived condition of the Mexican American and especially the Chicana. The second is language: the chapter printed here argues that a people's tongues are their identity and that their suppression is the deepest form of colonisation. The third is gender and sexuality, since Anzaldúa writes as a lesbian whose sexuality puts her outside both the Anglo and the Chicano communities. The fourth is survival, understood as the making of a self capable of living with unresolved contradiction rather than resolving it.
summary: The book opens with the image of the US-Mexico border as an open wound - '1,950 mile-long open wound' - where the First World grinds against the Third, and it returns to that image throughout. Its early chapters describe the author's childhood in the Rio Grande Valley, the shamans and folk healers of her family, and the history of the Mexican American dispossession of land in Texas after 1848. The middle chapters turn to the figures of female power that patriarchal culture has split into good and evil - the Virgin of Guadalupe, Malintzin (La Malinche) and Coatlicue, the serpent goddess - and argue for taking them back together. 'How to Tame a Wild Tongue' describes the punishments Anzaldúa received as a child for speaking Spanish at school and the varieties of Chicano Spanish she grew up inside, and concludes that until she can write in her own tongues she will be 'serving time' in others'. 'La conciencia de la mestiza' argues that the answer to the border's contradictions is not purity but a new consciousness that can hold incompatible things at once.
critical_context: The criticism is large and divided between celebration and qualification: it is credited with opening queer Chicana subjectivity and criticised, by later scholars, for an essentialist account of the indigenous past and for the relative absence of class analysis. Its bilingual practice is the most discussed feature, since the book declines to translate and thereby constitutes an English-reading audience that must tolerate not understanding.
research_notes: The book was not read in full for this record. The description of chapters five and seven rests on the published text of those chapters as quoted in criticism and anthologies; the order and argument of the opening chapters are given from the standard accounts of the book's structure.

title: Everyday Use
description: 'Everyday Use' was first published in Alice Walker's collection In Love & Trouble: Stories of Black Women (New York: Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1973) and is the most anthologised of her stories. It is a first-person narrative spoken by a rural Georgia mother about a single afternoon's visit from her elder daughter, and it turns on the meaning of two quilts.
plot_or_argument: The story is built as a test of three kinds of relation to the past, and its irony is that the one who has left is the one who cannot use it. Dee's return is a performance of heritage: she photographs the objects she would not have been seen dead beside as a child, she has changed her name to an invented African one without knowing its meaning, and she wants the quilts as objects to preserve rather than as things whose use is their meaning. Mrs Johnson is the story's moral centre and its narrator, and her narration is deliberately unliterary - she describes herself as a big-boned woman with hands like a man's, she is ironic about her education and her daughter's, and she judges without commenting. The story's most famous gesture is the mother's decision to give the quilts to Maggie, who will use them, rather than to Dee, who will hang them; and its most important technical feature is that the decision is made in the story rather than the story being told about it. Walker has said that the story came from watching Black students of the late 1960s reject their own families' culture while claiming an African one, and the story is careful to make Dee intelligent, brave and articulate rather than a fool: what she lacks is not politics but a relation to the people who made the things she wants.
narrative_structure: A single continuous first-person narrative in a rural Southern idiom, with one scene and no flashback; the story's structure is the long wait, the arrival, the meal and the quarrel, with the climax placed in a single gesture near the end.
meter_and_prosody: First-person vernacular narration, with an uneducated grammar that is consistent and unpatronised; free indirect speech for Dee; images drawn from the farm (the churn, the dasher, the yard, the bench); and an absence of metaphor, so that the quilts are simply quilts and carry the meaning by being described.
historical_context: The story appeared in 1973, in the years when Black Studies programmes and the Black Arts Movement had made 'heritage' a public question and when many African American writers were debating whether the rural southern past was a burden or a resource. Walker had worked in Mississippi in the civil rights movement and had written the story, she said, out of that experience; In Love & Trouble was her second book of fiction and her first collection of stories.
literary_significance: 'Everyday Use' is one of the two or three most widely taught stories in twentieth-century American literature and the standard text for the argument between a usable and an ornamental heritage. It is the story through which the Norton Anthology of American Literature represents Walker, and its title phrase has passed into the criticism as a term of value.
bibliographical_notes: First published in In Love & Trouble: Stories of Black Women (New York: Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1973); collected in The Complete Stories (1994). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the difference between heritage as a possession and heritage as a practice, carried by the quilts themselves, which are both art and bedding. The second is class: Dee's education has removed her from the poverty her mother still lives in, and the story refuses to say that this was simply a loss. The third is the Black family under segregation and its aftermath, and the forms of dignity available to a woman who has cleaned other people's houses. The fourth is naming, since Dee's renaming is the story's sharpest image of a politics that has detached itself from its inheritance.
summary: The narrator, Mrs Johnson, waits in the yard of the house she and her younger daughter Maggie live in for the visit of Dee, the elder daughter, who has been away at college and now calls herself Wangero Leewanika Kemanjo, saying that Dee is a name given by white people. Dee arrives with a male companion and photographs the house, the bench, the churn and the dasher as specimens of a folk past. At dinner she takes the butter dish and then the two quilts, made by her grandmother and aunt from scraps of dresses and Civil War uniforms, and announces that she will hang them. Her mother says that Maggie has been promised them and that Maggie can quilt more; Dee says Maggie would put them to 'everyday use' and that they are priceless. The mother takes the quilts out of Dee's hands and gives them to Maggie, and the story ends with the two of them sitting in the yard until it is time to go to bed.
critical_context: Criticism reads the story through the quilts, and the standard reading is that Maggie's use embodies a living tradition while Dee's display embalms it; a substantial counter-reading complicates the position by noting the story's own narrated hostility and the narrow options available to Maggie within it. Walker's own later description of the story as a product of the civil rights years is usually cited, and the story is regularly paired with her essay 'In Search of Our Mothers' Gardens', which the anthology also prints.
research_notes: The story was read for this record from its published text, but the Harcourt first edition was not examined and the exact page is not given. The date of first publication is the collection's 1973 imprint.

title: In Search of Our Mothers' Gardens: Womanist Prose
description: 'In Search of Our Mothers' Gardens' is the title essay of Alice Walker's collection of essays and journals, published by Harcourt Brace Jovanovich in 1983; the essay itself appeared in Ms. magazine in 1974, and the Norton dates the selection from that first periodical publication. It is the essay in which Walker's term 'womanist' is prepared, and its subject is the creative lives of Black women who were denied the chance to make art.
plot_or_argument: The essay's argument is that a tradition can exist without documents: if the forms in which Black women made things - gardens, quilts, songs, cooking - were not recognised as art, that is a fact about the recognition, not about the making. Walker's method is to read her mother's life as a text: the garden is a poem, the quilt is a composition, and the values of beauty, spirituality and self-respect that they embodied were the inheritance she received. The move is characteristically double. It is a recovery of the lives of Black women who left no books, and it is a rebuke to a feminist criticism that had defined creativity by the conditions of white middle-class authorship - Walker quotes Woolf's account of the woman who would have written Shakespeare's plays and observes that for the Black woman the obstacles were not a room and an income but slavery and forced labour. The essay is also where the word 'womanist', which Walker would define formally in the same collection, begins to do work: a Black feminism that includes the love of women, of music, of the folk, of herself. Its tone is essayistic and personal rather than polemical; the authority is in the family example.
narrative_structure: A single essay of roughly twenty pages, organised as a sequence of exempla - Toomer's butterflies, the author's mother, Wheatley, Woolf - each of which sharpens the argument, closing on the author's own inheritance rather than on a conclusion.
literary_form: Essay (title essay, collected in book of the same name, 1983)
meter_and_prosody: Personal and essayistic; a plain declarative sentence with a strong rhythmic close; quotations from Toomer and Woolf used as countervoices; first person throughout; and an absence of theory vocabulary, so that the argument is carried by example.
historical_context: The essay appeared in Ms. in 1974, in the first years of the magazine's influence, and was collected in 1983, when Black feminist criticism was defining itself in books such as Barbara Smith's Toward a Black Feminist Criticism and bell hooks's Ain't I a Woman. Walker's term 'womanist' - defined in the collection's front matter - was taken up across the academy and in Black theology, and the essay's title has become a standard phrase for the recovery of women's unrecorded work.
literary_significance: The essay is one of the texts that established Black feminist criticism as a field, and its garden has become the governing image for a whole tradition of recovery scholarship; 'womanist' has entered the lexicon of theology and criticism. The Norton prints it beside 'Everyday Use', which is a recognition that Walker's fiction and her criticism make the same argument by different means.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Ms. magazine in 1974; collected as the title essay of In Search of Our Mothers' Gardens: Womanist Prose (New York: Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1983). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the creativity of Black women in conditions that forbade its public exercise, and the essay's whole force is in refusing to call that creativity thwarted. The second is the relation of Black women to a white feminist tradition, which Walker reads as well-meaning and incomplete. The third is motherhood and inheritance, since the essay's structure is a daughter's reading of her mother's life. The fourth is the politics of acceptable art, and the pressure on Black writers to be representative.
summary: The essay begins with a quotation from Jean Toomer's Cane describing Black women in the 1920s as 'exquisite butterflies trapped in an evil honey', and asks what happened to the creative power of such women. Walker answers with the figure of her own mother, a sharecropper's wife who worked in the fields, bore eight children, sewed quilts and made a garden of flowers wherever the family stopped. She argues that the artist in such a woman was driven underground into the only forms allowed her - the garden, the quilt, the story told to a child - and that the 'anonymity' of those forms is not an absence of art but its condition. The essay moves through Phillis Wheatley, who had to write hymns; through Virginia Woolf's argument in A Room of One's Own and its blind spot about Black women; and through the example of the Black community's expectation that its artists be acceptable and respectable. It closes with Walker's sense that her own work is the continuation of her mother's gardens.
critical_context: Criticism reads the essay as the founding statement of womanist thought and as a correction to Woolf, and its central image has been widely adopted - most influentially in the title of Walker's own collection and in the subsequent scholarship on Black women's quilting. Some later critics have questioned the essay's reliance on a redemptive reading of suffering, and the term womanist has been debated and revised by Black queer and trans writers.
research_notes: The essay was read for this record from the collected text; the Ms. appearance of 1974 is given from the collection's own acknowledgements as repeated in the standard bibliographies. The anthology's date of 1974 follows the periodical publication, which precedes the book.

title: Fences
description: Fences was first performed at the Yale Repertory Theatre in 1985 and opened on Broadway in 1987, where it won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama and the Tony Award for Best Play. It is the sixth play of August Wilson's ten-play Pittsburgh or Century Cycle, set in 1957 in the Hill District, and it is the work through which the Norton Anthology of American Literature represents him.
plot_or_argument: The play's structure is domestic and its argument is historical, and Wilson's method is to let the history arrive through the ordinary speech of the yard. Troy is a man of great vitality and great damage: his stories of the Negro Leagues, of his father's brutality and of his own time in prison are the play's music, and his refusal of Cory's scholarship is both a jealous insistence that his son not have what he was denied and a genuinely protective fear that a Black athlete will be discarded again. The fence of the title is built across both acts and means different things to each character - Rose's enclosure of her family, Troy's unfinished defence, Cory's barrier - and Wilson uses it as the play's single stage symbol without forcing it into an allegory. The play's most important move is theological: Troy wrestles with Death as an actual presence throughout, in the manner of a blues singer's boast, and the ending, in which Gabriel's horn-trumpet at the funeral blows open the gates of heaven, gives that boast a ritual answer. Wilson's language is the play's achievement: long monologues in the cadences of 1950s Black Pittsburgh speech, with the blues, the union and baseball as a shared vocabulary, and an ear for the moment when a joke turns into a wound.
narrative_structure: Two acts in a single unit set, the backyard of the Maxson house, with the fence under construction across both acts; the action moves through a series of conversations and confrontations rather than a plotted intrigue, and the climax is a domestic quarrel rather than a public event; a funeral and a child's birth enclose the end.
meter_and_prosody: Naturalistic dialogue in Black Pittsburgh speech, with long arias of monologue; the blues and the Negro Leagues as the play's shared cultural reference; a single symbolic object on stage; and a mixture of realistic detail with a mythic register in Troy's addresses to Death.
historical_context: Fences was written in the mid-1980s as the sixth of Wilson's cycle and premiered at Yale Rep in 1985 before its 1987 Broadway production with James Earl Jones, which made Wilson a national figure; the play's 1957 setting is the year the civil rights movement reached Little Rock and the year before the integration of major-league baseball's southern spring training. It was revived on Broadway in 2010 with Denzel Washington and filmed in 2016 with the same actor and Viola Davis.
literary_significance: Fences is the most honoured American play of its decade and the one through which Wilson is known to readers who do not go to the theatre; the Century Cycle as a whole is generally described as the most sustained dramatic project in American literature, and Fences is its most performed play. The Norton's inclusion of it makes the anthology's American volume a record of drama as well as of poetry and fiction in the period.
bibliographical_notes: First performed at the Yale Repertory Theatre in 1985; published by New American Library (Plume) in 1986 and opened on Broadway at the 46th Street Theatre in March 1987. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the inheritance of slavery and the colour line as it operates in ordinary life: Troy's baseball career is the play's image of a meritocracy that was never open to him. The second is fatherhood and the reproduction of damage, since Troy repeats on Cory the violence his own father used on him and knows that he is doing it. The third is Rose's claim to dignity and her insistence on responsibility, which is the play's moral centre. The fourth is death, which Troy personifies and fights, and which the play treats as a social fact - the deaths of Black men - as well as a mythic one.
summary: Troy Maxson, fifty-two, is a sanitation worker in Pittsburgh who collects garbage from the back of a truck and has spent years fighting the union's refusal to let Black men drive. He was a powerful baseball player in the Negro Leagues before the colour line kept him out of the majors, he served time in prison for a killing committed in a robbery, and he has built a life with his wife Rose and his sons Lyons, Cory and Gabriel. Over two acts he refuses to let Cory accept a college football scholarship, tells Rose that he has fathered a child with another woman, fights his son physically, and is left at the end of the play with a baby daughter, Raynell, whom Rose agrees to raise, standing in a yard where the fence he was building is at last finished; Cory returns from the Marines and refuses, at first, to go to his father's funeral.
critical_context: Criticism reads the play through the fence, through Troy's relation to the blues and to Death, and through Wilson's argument, set out in his 1996 essay 'The Ground on Which I Stand', that African American theatre needs Black institutions rather than integration into white ones. The standard critique - that Wilson's women are given less interiority than his men - was sharpened by later criticism of the cycle, while Rose's part in Fences is generally exempted from it.
research_notes: The premiere and Broadway dates are given from the standard production record; the play's text was not read in full for this record, and the account of the plot rests on its published text and on the standard critical summaries. The 1986 New American Library publication date is that of the first edition.

title: How to Tell a True War Story
description: 'How to Tell a True War Story' was first published in Esquire in October 1987 and collected in The Things They Carried (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1990), where it is the seventh of twenty-two linked stories. It is the most discussed American short story about the Vietnam War, and it is as much an essay on storytelling as a story.
plot_or_argument: The story is a demonstration of its own thesis, which is that a war story's truth is not the accuracy of its events. The narrative is broken into short numbered sections that move between anecdote and aphorism, and the narrator repeatedly interrupts his own telling to comment on it, so that the reader is never allowed to settle into believing what is told. The famous sentences are the ones that state the paradox: 'A true war story is never moral', 'you can tell a true war story by the questions you ask', 'in a true war story nothing is ever absolutely true'. O'Brien's method is to make the reader feel the difference between happening-truth and story-truth, the first being what occurred and the second being what the telling makes real, and to argue that only the second can carry the war to someone who was not there. The water buffalo passage is the story's most disturbing sequence and its clearest example: the torture of the animal is not explained, and its absence of explanation is offered as the definition of a true war story. The ending, in which the narrator addresses the reader directly and tells her that she is the audience for a story she cannot hear, completes the argument by moving the problem of testimony into the act of reading.
narrative_structure: A sequence of short numbered sections alternating between anecdotes and rules, with the narrator interrupting his own narrative; no single plot, and an ending that addresses the reader rather than closing the story.
meter_and_prosody: A plain, declarative American sentence; direct address to the reader; aphorism used as structure; repetition of key statements with variation; and a refusal of figurative heightening at the moments of greatest violence.
historical_context: The story appeared in Esquire in 1987 and in book form in 1990, fifteen years after the end of the Vietnam War and in the year of the Gulf War's build-up; it belongs to a late phase of American Vietnam writing in which the war is treated as a problem of memory and representation rather than of combat. O'Brien served in Vietnam in 1969-70 and the collection's narrator shares his name and much of his biography, which has made the stories' status a continuing critical question.
literary_significance: The story is the central text in the American literature of the Vietnam War and one of the standard examples in discussions of metafiction and of testimony; its formulations are quoted in historiography and journalism as well as in literary criticism. The Norton prints it as a story in its own right, which treats a chapter of a linked collection as a discrete literary work.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Esquire, October 1987; collected in The Things They Carried (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1990). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the relation of truth to fiction, treated not as a philosophical puzzle but as a soldier's practical problem. The second is grief and the failure of consolation, figured in the unanswered letter to Lemon's sister. The third is the incommunicability of combat and the obligation to try to communicate it anyway. The fourth is memory, since the story insists that what is remembered changes and that the change is not a corruption but the material.
summary: The narrator, named Tim O'Brien, tells of the death of his friend Curt Lemon, killed by a booby-trapped 105-mm round while playing catch with Rat Kiley, and of Rat Kiley's letter to Lemon's sister, who never answers. He tells of a listening post in the mountains where the soldiers hear music and voices in the dark and call in artillery on a silence, and the company's CO orders them to keep listening. He tells the story of the water buffalo, which Rat Kiley tortures and shoots after Lemon's death. Between the stories he states rules: that a true war story is never moral, that it cannot be believed and cannot be doubted, that if it seems moral do not believe it, that in a true war story nothing much happens, and that the ending is not the point. He admits that he has told the story of Lemon's death differently at different times - the booby trap, the sunlight, the smoke - and says that the story he tells now is the one that is truest.
critical_context: Criticism reads the story with the collection's other metafictional pieces and debates whether its narrator's admissions make it more or less reliable; the standard account treats the happening-truth and story-truth distinction as the collection's governing idea. Historians of the war have cited it as evidence of how soldiers' memories work, and the story is regularly taught in courses on trauma and on the ethics of representation.
research_notes: The Esquire appearance of 1987 is the earliest publication found and is the date the Norton list carries; the story's text was read from the 1990 collection, which may differ from the magazine version.

title: Facing It
description: 'Facing It' is the closing poem of Dien Cai Dau (Middletown: Wesleyan University Press, 1988), Yusef Komunyakaa's book about his service in Vietnam. It describes a visit to the Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Washington and is the most anthologised American poem about that war.
plot_or_argument: The poem's subject is that seeing the memorial is not a single act, and its technique is the double exposure of reflection and inscription. Komunyakaa uses the wall's mirror surface to put the living and the dead in one plane, so that the poem's 'I' is simultaneously the viewer outside the wall and a name inside it. The line 'I'm stone. I'm flesh' is the whole argument in four words, and the poem does not resolve it: the speaker moves between identifying with the dead and being restored to his body by ordinary life - the woman and the boy. The poem's racial thinking is carried by 'my black face' in the first line and by the 'white vet's image' in the middle, so that the memorial's promise of a common sacrifice is placed against the difference the war also enforced. The ending is a correction of vision: what looks like a woman erasing names is a woman brushing a boy's hair, which means that the poem's grief is interrupted by the ordinary, and that the interruption is the poem's consolation without being its resolution. The form is short free-verse lines with abrupt enjambment, and the economy is extreme: the whole poem is under forty lines, and almost every line contains a verb of seeing. It is the one poem in Dien Cai Dau to make the memorial itself the subject, and that choice - to write about the wall rather than about the fighting - is what has kept it in circulation.
narrative_structure: A single unbroken lyric of short lines, organised by the alternation of what is seen in the stone and what is seen in the world, ending on a correction of the poem's own image.
meter_and_prosody: Very short free-verse lines; present-tense perception; enjambment that forces the reader to hold two meanings at once; almost no adjectives of feeling; and a vocabulary drawn from light, stone and water rather than from combat.
historical_context: The Vietnam Veterans Memorial, designed by Maya Lin, was dedicated in 1982, and the poem was written in the mid-1980s and published in Dien Cai Dau in 1988, when public commemoration of Vietnam service had become a national argument. Komunyakaa served in Vietnam as an army correspondent in 1969-70 and has said he could not write about it for years; the book's title is the soldiers' slang phrase for a dead or crazy comrade.
literary_significance: 'Facing It' is the American poem about the Vietnam War most often taught and anthologised, and it is the poem by which Komunyakaa's generation of Vietnam veterans' writing is represented in the Norton; its lines are quoted in criticism on memorials, race and American memory. Its presence in the anthology's period gives the war a poem as well as a story, alongside O'Brien's.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Dien Cai Dau (Middletown, CT: Wesleyan University Press, 1988); collected in Neon Vernacular (1993) and Pleasure Dome (2001). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the Vietnam Veterans Memorial itself and the way its design - black granite, names in chronological order, no commentary - makes mourning a reflective act. The second is the survivor's guilt, since the speaker is alive and his reflection proves it. The third is race, since a Black veteran at the wall is a reminder of who fought and who is remembered. The fourth is the ordinary life that continues beside the monument, carried by the woman and the boy.
summary: The poem begins 'My black face fades, / hiding inside the black granite', and its speaker stands at the wall reading names. The reflection in the polished stone keeps interfering with what he sees: his own face and the names are on the same surface, a woman is brushing a boy's hair in the reflection, and a white vet's image floats beside him. He touches a name and the poem's most quoted line follows - 'I'm stone. I'm flesh.' - and the poem moves between the two states for its remainder: he sees the dead in the wall, he watches a plane in the sky, and at the end he is 'inside the Vietnam Veterans Memorial' watching the reflection of a woman trying to erase names, and the poem closes 'No, she's brushing a boy's hair'.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem's mirror structure as its argument - the reflection makes the viewer part of the monument - and discusses 'I'm stone. I'm flesh' as a condensation of the veteran's double existence; the racial reading, centred on the black granite and the black face, has been developed by critics writing on African American war poetry. The closing correction is generally read as the poem's refusal of closure.
research_notes: The poem was read for this record from its published text; the anthology's page reference and the date of the poem's first magazine appearance, if any, were not established.

title: Slam, Dunk, & Hook
description: 'Slam, Dunk, & Hook' was first published in Callaloo in the summer of 1991 and collected in Magic City (Middletown: Wesleyan University Press, 1992), Komunyakaa's book of Bogalusa childhood. It is a poem about boys playing basketball, and it is the best-known example of his use of sport as a form of lyric knowledge.
plot_or_argument: The poem is about the beauty of a game played by boys who have nothing else, and it refuses the obvious irony that would point out the limits of basketball as a way out of poverty. Komunyakaa's method is to write the game as if it were a mythology, with Mercury's winged sneakers and angels in mid-air, and then to bring it back to the ordinary world without deflating it: the boys are sons of angels who also eat glazed doughnuts. The poem's politics are implicit in the myth's materials. The gods are named through their commercial logos, the flight is the flight of Black boys in a small Southern town in the segregation years, and the 'secret stories' the players carry are connected to the rest of Magic City, whose poems record the terror and the beauty of Bogalusa together. The rhythm is the poem's real argument: short lines with heavy stresses that mimic the stops and breaks of the game, so that reading it is closer to performing it than to describing it. The close is a deliberate return - the players come down to the ground, the poem ends, the game is over - and it is that return that keeps the poem from being sentimental about sport.
narrative_structure: A single free-verse lyric in short lines, organised by the movement of a game from fast break to final return, with no stanza division beyond the poem's own turns.
meter_and_prosody: Short lines with hard stresses; present tense and first-person plural; proper names and brand names used as mythic material; a jazz-like syntax that drops subjects; and an early rhyme of the sacred with the commercial.
historical_context: Magic City appeared in 1992, the year after Callaloo printed the poem, and belongs to the period in which Komunyakaa was writing two books at once - Dien Cai Dau about the war and Magic City about the South. Its Bogalusa is the mill town of his childhood, and the poem's publication in Callaloo places it in the leading journal of African American literary criticism and writing.
literary_significance: The poem is one of the most anthologised American poems about sport and the standard example of Komunyakaa's early style; it is a Norton selection, and its pairing with 'Facing It' shows the two poles of the anthology's representation of him - the war and the boyhood that preceded it.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Callaloo 14.3 (Summer 1991), pp. 631-632; collected in Magic City (Middletown, CT: Wesleyan University Press, 1992) and Pleasure Dome (2001). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is adolescence and physical joy, and the poem is unusual in American poetry for describing athletic beauty without condescension. The second is race and the segregated South in which these boys play. The third is the relation of play to art, since the poem treats the game as a composed thing with its own form. The fourth is escape, held in tension with the town the boys cannot actually leave.
summary: The poem opens with 'Fast breaks. Lay ups. With Mercury's / Insignia on our sneakers', and it calls the players 'the sons of angels, / gone dazzling in mid-air'. Its boys play on a court and in a game that is half myth - 'we were dangerous', they wore 'our secret stories' like sweat - and the poem's images are of flight, of the body outwitting gravity, and of the game as an escape from the town as well as a spell held inside it. It ends with the speakers 'glistening like a glazed donut' and back on the ground, the court returning to its ordinary place.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem's mythologising of the playground as a characteristic Komunyakaa move, and discusses it with the basketball poems of other Black poets; the standard reading is that the poem's classical reference is not ornamental but a claim about the value of the boys' play. The Callaloo bibliography records its first appearance.
research_notes: The Callaloo first appearance is from the Michael Collins bibliography of Komunyakaa in Callaloo; the poem's text was read from the collection, not from the journal.

title: My Father's Love Letters
description: 'My Father's Love Letters' is in Magic City (Middletown: Wesleyan University Press, 1992), Komunyakaa's second book of Bogalusa poems. It is a short narrative lyric about a boy writing letters for his illiterate father, and it is among his most personal poems.
plot_or_argument: The poem's subject is not infidelity but power, and its technique is to keep the child's point of view while letting the reader see what the child does not. The father cannot write, so the son's literacy makes him both necessary and complicit: he is the hand of his father's desire and the witness of his mother's injury. Komunyakaa's short lines and his refusal to comment allow the scene to stand as an image rather than a judgement, and the poem's restraint is what makes it painful. The larger subject is the household of a Black working family in the segregated South, where the father's word is the only authority available to him in a world that gives him none, and where his son's education is at once his pride and the means of his exposure. The poem is also, quietly, about writing: the son's first literary act is a love letter dictated by someone else, and the poem records the origin of a writer's relation to language in service to another person's need.
narrative_structure: A short free-verse narrative in a single remembered scene, with the dictation as its organising action and a closing movement into the speaker's adult understanding.
meter_and_prosody: Short unpunctuated lines; concrete domestic objects; the father's speech rendered in direct quotation against the son's silence; and a syntax that withholds judgement to the end.
historical_context: Magic City (1992) collects the Bogalusa material Komunyakaa had been writing since Copacetic (1984), and the book's Southern mill town is treated with the same historical attention he gave the war in Dien Cai Dau. The poem's illiterate father and literate son belong to the first generation of Black Southerners with access to schooling after segregation, and the poem's situation is a common one in African American memoir.
literary_significance: The poem is one of the most frequently anthologised in Magic City and is regularly taught as an example of the narrative lyric in contemporary African American poetry; the Norton's selection of it with 'Slam, Dunk, & Hook' gives the anthology both the public and the domestic sides of the book.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Magic City (Middletown, CT: Wesleyan University Press, 1992); collected in Pleasure Dome (2001). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the father-son relation, held between love and coercion. The second is the mother's position, present in the poem mostly through what is not said to her. The third is literacy as a form of power inside a family that has been denied it publicly. The fourth is the making of a writer, since the poem is an account of the first time the speaker used writing for someone else.
summary: The poem's speaker, as a boy, is asked to write love letters for his father, who cannot write them himself: the father dictates, the son writes, and the letters are sent to women. The poem describes the father's authority in the house, the mother's silence and labour, and the son's position as the instrument through which the father speaks to other women. Its images are domestic and exact - the table, the paper, the dictation - and the poem closes with the son grown, understanding what he was made to do and what it cost the household.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem with the other family poems of Magic City and notes its treatment of literacy as an inheritance; the standard account of Komunyakaa's development places the Bogalusa poems as the ground from which the Vietnam book was written, since he wrote about the town before he could write about the war.
research_notes: The poem's first periodical appearance, if any, was not established; the date given is that of the collection, which is the earliest publication found.

title: Nude Study
description: 'Nude Study' was first published in Poetry in the winter of 1992 and collected in Taboo: The Wishbone Trilogy, Part One (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2004). It is a poem about a painting - John Singer Sargent's studies of the Black model Thomas Eugene McKeller - and it appeared in Poetry in 1992 and was collected twelve years later.
plot_or_argument: The poem is an ekphrasis that turns into an argument about appropriation, and its charge comes from the fact that Sargent's drawings are genuinely beautiful. Komunyakaa does not resolve the contradiction between the aesthetic value of the work and the erasure it performs; he lets both stand, and the poem's intelligence is in its refusal of an easy verdict. The figures are classical - the murals depict Greek myth and the figures of the library - so that McKeller's body is recruited into a European tradition that would not have admitted him as a person, and the poem's title names the problem: a 'study' is a painter's preparation, an exercise in seeing, and the poem is a study of that study. Komunyakaa's late style is much more discursive than the short lyric of Magic City, with long sentences and an essayistic movement, and 'Nude Study' is a characteristic example: it thinks in public about the ethics of looking, and the first person of the Black viewer is placed against the white painter's gaze.
narrative_structure: An ekphrastic lyric that moves between description and commentary, with no stanza break marking a change of argument and no resolution at the close.
meter_and_prosody: Discursive free verse with long sentences and Latinate vocabulary; ekphrastic description that keeps the painter's technique in view; a first-person viewer who is also a critic; and an absence of irony.
historical_context: Sargent painted the McKeller studies in 1917-20 for the murals of the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston and Harvard's Widener Library, and McKeller's identity as the model became a subject of art history and public discussion in the 1990s and after. Komunyakaa's poem appeared in Poetry in the winter of 1992 and was collected, with revisions and a trilogy's architecture around it, in Taboo (2004); the 1992 periodical publication is the first and is the date recorded here.
literary_significance: The poem is the most discussed piece in Taboo and a standard text in the art-history and literature of the Black model. Its 1992 magazine publication puts it inside the anthology's period even though the book it is known from appeared in 2004 - a case of the anthology printing an old poem in a new book, which is exactly why the record dates the first printing and names the collection separately.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Poetry (Winter 1992); collected in Taboo: The Wishbone Trilogy, Part One (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2004). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the erasure of the Black model in Western art, and the poem's specific case is the classical nude. The second is the ethics of aesthetic pleasure, since the poem admits to admiring what it criticises. The third is race and the classical tradition, which the murals' use of McKeller makes unavoidable. The fourth is the act of looking itself, which the poem treats as a transaction between unequal parties.
summary: The poem looks at Sargent's nude studies of Thomas E. McKeller, the African American bellhop and elevator operator from Boston who modelled for the murals Sargent painted for the Museum of Fine Arts and Harvard's Widener Library, and whose body was used for the classical and mythological figures in those murals. The poem describes the drawings' beauty and the conditions of their making: a Black man's body made into the white classical ideal, a model paid for his pose and unnamed in the work, and a painter using him as a means. It holds admiration for the drawing against the knowledge of what the drawing does.
critical_context: Art historians and critics have written on the McKeller studies since the 1990s, and Komunyakaa's poem is regularly cited in that discussion as the literary treatment of them; the standard reading of Taboo treats the trilogy as an attempt to write a history of race and art in the West, with 'Nude Study' as its most concentrated example.
research_notes: The Poetry appearance of winter 1992 is the earliest publication found and is the date recorded; the 2004 book is named as the collection the poem is known from. The Norton list carried the poem as undated before this wave.

title: Maus
description: Maus is Art Spiegelman's two-volume graphic narrative of his father's survival of the Holocaust, in which Jews are drawn as mice, Germans as cats and Poles as pigs. Its first six chapters were serialised in RAW from 1980 and published as Maus I: A Survivor's Tale - My Father Bleeds History (New York: Pantheon, 1986); the remainder appeared as Maus II: A Survivor's Tale - And Here My Troubles Began (Pantheon, 1991). The Norton prints chapter six, 'Mousetrap', from the first volume.
plot_or_argument: The book's formal invention is the animal mask, and its effect is not allegory but estrangement: the reader is made to see that the categories of the Holocaust were themselves a way of sorting beings into species that could be killed without it counting as murder. Spiegelman complicates the scheme deliberately - there are Jewish mice who behave like cats, Poles in pig masks who save and betray, and in the second volume a German-Jewish couple, and Spiegelman himself in a mouse mask wearing a prisoner's uniform in 'Prisoner on the Hell Planet'. The second innovation is the doubling of time. Vladek's story is never given alone; it competes with the present-day errands and quarrels, and the reader sees that the father's survivor's habits - hoarding, penny-pinching, an inability to throw anything away - are the war continuing in a Queens apartment. The third is the book's admission of its own inadequacy: Artie is told by a survivor that Auschwitz has no place for cartoon mice, and the second volume includes 'Time Flies', in which the success of the first book is treated as a kind of fraud. The drawing is crude in the manner of the underground comix Spiegelman came from, and the crude mask is what allows the book to escape both the reverence and the kitsch of Holocaust representation.
narrative_structure: Two volumes of serialised chapters, each alternating the present-day interview with the wartime narrative, with the frame itself becoming a subject in the second volume; page layouts of varying panel sizes rather than a rigid grid, and a long silent 'Prisoner on the Hell Planet' inset.
literary_form: Graphic novel / graphic memoir (two volumes, 1986 and 1991)
meter_and_prosody: Black-and-white brush and ink; anthropomorphic masks that are never explained; a visual vocabulary borrowed from the newspaper strip and the underground comix; handwritten narration boxes; and a deliberate roughness that refuses the polish of the memorial book.
historical_context: The book grew out of a three-page strip, 'Maus', published in the underground magazine Funny Animals in 1972, and was serialised in RAW, the comics journal Spiegelman founded with Françoise Mouly, from 1980; the first collection appeared in 1986 and the second in 1991, and the completed work won a special Pulitzer Prize in 1992. Its publication coincided with the growth of Holocaust memory in the United States, the opening of the US Holocaust Memorial Museum (1993) and the academic legitimation of comics.
literary_significance: Maus won the first Pulitzer Prize ever given to a comic and is the work through which the graphic novel became a subject of literary and historical study; it is taught in history departments as well as literature ones, and its animal masks are a standard example in discussions of representation and the Shoah. The Norton's selection of a single chapter places a comic - unmistakably a comic, with speech balloons - inside the American literary canon of the period, which is the anthology's largest single formal statement.
bibliographical_notes: Serialised in RAW (1980-91); published as Maus I (New York: Pantheon, 1986) and Maus II (Pantheon, 1991); collected as Maus: A Survivor's Tale (1992). The Norton prints chapter six, 'Mousetrap', from the first volume. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the Holocaust itself, told in the specific and personal terms of one family rather than as historical summary. The second is the transmission of trauma to the second generation, since Artie is the book's real narrator and his inheritance is the book. The third is the ethics of representation: how, and whether, atrocity can be drawn. The fourth is the ordinary present, in which the survivor's household is both comic and wounding, and which the book insists on placing beside the camps.
summary: The frame is the present: Artie, the cartoonist, visits his father Vladek in Rego Park, Queens, and coaxes from him the story of the war. Inside the frame, Vladek's narrative runs from the courtship of his wife Anja in Sosnowiec, through the ghetto, the hiding places, the betrayal and the transports, to Auschwitz and Dachau and the death marches at the end of the war. Chapter six, 'Mousetrap', moves between the present-day household - Vladek's second wife Mala, his miserliness, his heart condition, his need for Artie's attention - and the wartime story, in which Vladek and Anja are hidden by Polish families and finally betrayed by one of them. The volume ends with Vladek burning Anja's diaries and with the couple's arrival at Auschwitz.
critical_context: The critical literature is very large: it includes Holocaust studies work on the ethics of comic-form testimony, comics scholarship on the animal mask and on layout, and the controversy over a 1991 review in The Village Voice. The standard reading treats the father-son frame as the book's true subject, with the camps narrated in order that the present can be understood; 'Mousetrap' is the chapter usually cited for the interleaving of the two times.
research_notes: The exact page range of 'Mousetrap' in the anthology was not established. The chapter numbering and the placement of Anja's diaries and the arrival at Auschwitz at the end of volume one are given from the published book.

title: ¡Yo!
description: ¡Yo! (Chapel Hill: Algonquin Books, 1997) is Julia Alvarez's second novel about the García family of How the García Girls Lost Their Accents (1991). It tells the story of the second sister, Yolanda, entirely through the voices of the people around her, and the Norton prints its chapter 'The Mother'.
plot_or_argument: The novel's structure is its argument. By refusing Yolanda a first-person chapter, Alvarez makes the immigrant writer's identity a composite of other people's descriptions, which is the condition the book is about: Yolanda is an American writer to her Dominican family and a Dominican daughter to her American friends, and neither account is complete. The mother's chapter is the emotional centre of the novel because it is told by the person with the strongest claim to know her, and because Laura's account is loving and uncomprehending at the same time. Alvarez handles the mother's voice with great care: Laura is not a villain and not a saint, she is a woman of a certain class and generation whose daughter's freedoms - sexual, literary, linguistic - are real gains and real losses at once. The novel's comedy comes from the chorus of narrators, each convinced that Yolanda is the problem and that they are the solution; its sorrow comes from the recognition that no single narrator, including the mother, can hold her. The book's bilingual title and its untranslated Spanish are part of the same argument about a life lived in two languages, and 'The Mother' is the chapter in which the gap between the languages is most painfully marked.
narrative_structure: A sequence of first-person chapters each spoken by a different character, with Yolanda herself withheld; no single plotline, and a chronology that returns to the same events from different angles; the mother's chapter is one of the longest.
literary_form: Novel (multi-voice, told by a chorus of narrators)
meter_and_prosody: Each chapter in a distinct idiolect - Dominican Spanish-inflected English, academic English, child's English - with Spanish left unglossed; direct address and conversational framing; and a comic timing learnt from the family anecdote.
historical_context: ¡Yo! appeared in 1997, three years after In the Time of the Butterflies and six after How the García Girls Lost Their Accents, at a point when US Latina fiction had a mass readership; Algonquin Books was a small Southern press that had become a significant publisher of American fiction.
