The novel's multi-voice form belongs to the 1990s interest in polyphonic and testimonial narrative, and its Dominican material reflects the growth of the Dominican American community in New York after 1965.
literary_significance: The novel is a standard example of the polyphonic immigrant novel and is regularly taught alongside García Girls, which it revises; 'The Mother' is the chapter most often anthologised because it gives the mother's voice that the earlier novel does not. The Norton's selection of it registers the 1990s as a decade of US Latina writing and Alvarez as one of its central practitioners.
bibliographical_notes: First published by Algonquin Books of Chapel Hill in 1997. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E, which prints the chapter 'The Mother'.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is immigration and the family that remains behind, treated from the mother's side as well as the daughter's. The second is bilingualism and the loss of intimacy that comes with a new language. The third is the position of a woman writer inside a traditional family, and the cost of her autonomy to her mother. The fourth is narrative authority itself, since the novel is about who is allowed to tell a life.
summary: The novel's premise is that everyone has a version of Yolanda except Yolanda, who is writing a novel in the third person and appearing only in other people's chapters. Her sisters, her cousins, her lovers, her teachers, her Dominican family's servants, her American landlords and her psychiatrist each narrate a section, and the composite portrait that emerges is of a woman divided by languages, loyalties and versions of herself. 'The Mother' is narrated by Yolanda's mother, Laura García, in the first person: she describes her daughter's return from college changed, her English, her refusal of the family's expectations, and her own bewilderment at a child who has become a stranger, and she measures the distance between the life she imagined for her daughter and the American one she has.
critical_context: Criticism reads the novel as a critique of the first-person authority of García Girls and as an experiment in collective narration; the standard account notes that by withholding Yolanda, Alvarez dramatises the impossibility of a single immigrant self. The mother's chapter is usually discussed for its sympathetic rendering of a figure who could easily have been an obstacle.
research_notes: The novel was not read in full for this record; 'The Mother' was read in its published form and the rest of the description rests on the standard accounts of the novel's structure. The chapter's page range in the anthology was not established.

title: Call It Fear
description: 'Call It Fear' opens She Had Some Horses (New York: Thunder's Mouth Press, 1983), the book that established Joy Harjo. It is a short poem spoken to the self about fear, and it sets the terms - a first person that is also a people, a past that will not stay past - for the whole collection.
plot_or_argument: 'Call It Fear' is a poem of naming, and its method is the Mvskoke and broadly Native American practice of speaking to a condition in order to place it outside the person. The fear is not analysed and its origins are not narrated; the poem proceeds as if the act of naming were itself the work, and the reader is placed in the position of the one who is told to speak. Harjo's short lines carry a great deal of white space, and the effect is of a voice thinking aloud in a room rather than declaring from a platform. The poem's historical dimension is implicit but unmistakable in the book's context: this is a Native woman's fear, in a country whose history has given her reasons for it, and the poem's refusal to explain is a refusal to make the fear legible for an outsider. What makes it survive as a poem rather than a statement is its rhythm - the repetition of the imperative, the short breath of the lines, the sense that the speaker is talking herself into the naming.
narrative_structure: A short free-verse poem in very short lines, built on an imperative address and repetition, with a turn toward release at the close rather than a narrative progression.
meter_and_prosody: Very short free-verse lines; plain diction; repetition and anaphora; direct address; and an absence of punctuation at the line ends, so that the poem moves by breath.
historical_context: She Had Some Horses appeared from Thunder's Mouth Press in 1983, the year of Harjo's MFA from Iowa and of the consolidation of the Native American Renaissance; the book's poems draw on Mvskoke ceremony, on the Oklahoma landscape and on the experience of a Native woman in the American West. Thunder's Mouth was the press that also published Ortiz's From Sand Creek and Harjo's own She Had Some Horses album material.
literary_significance: The poem opens the collection that made Harjo's name and is the standard entry point to her early work; its imperative address and its short line are the features her later poetry developed. It is a Norton selection and, with 'White Bear', represents the 1983 book in the anthology.
bibliographical_notes: First published in She Had Some Horses (New York: Thunder's Mouth Press, 1983); collected in How We Became Human: New and Selected Poems (New York: W. W. Norton, 2004). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is fear itself, treated as a physical and historical fact rather than a mood. The second is the relation of the present self to a violent past, which the poem holds without narrating. The third is gender, since the fear is a woman's and the collection's other poems make clear what has caused it. The fourth is survival, which the poem approaches through the act of speech.
summary: The poem addresses someone, probably the speaker herself, and tells them to call the thing they have been running from by its name: fear. It places the fear in a landscape - a road, a house, a night - and in a history, and it refuses to separate the two. Its lines are short and its language is plain, and the poem turns at the end toward the possibility of putting the fear down.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem as a ceremonial act of naming and places it in the tradition of Native women's writing about violence; the standard account of She Had Some Horses treats its opening as a threshold poem that establishes the collection's speaking position.
research_notes: The poem's text was read from the collection and the 2004 selected poems; the first periodical appearance, if any, was not established.

title: White Bear
description: 'White Bear' is in She Had Some Horses (New York: Thunder's Mouth Press, 1983). Harjo has said she wrote it in 1983, on the point of boarding a plane out of a city, and it is a visionary poem in which a white bear appears as a figure of balance and of the northern cold.
plot_or_argument: The poem is a dream narrative in which the dreaming mind is given the authority of a vision. The white bear is not explained and not identified with a particular tribal figure; it is a creature of the north, a moon and a cradle, and the poem's images accumulate rather than argue. That accumulation is Harjo's method in the early books: a sequence of luminous objects arranged so that the reader feels their relation before understanding it. The daughter's eyes in the middle of the poem make the vision domestic as well as cosmic, and the cradle image ties the movement of the northern sky to the rocking of a child. The ending is the poem's argument: the balance could tip either way, and the speaker chooses to say that darkness is open to light, which is a statement of survival made in the grammar of a blessing. The poem's landscape is not named as Oklahoma or Alaska but as a dream's north, and its power comes from the refusal to localise the myth.
narrative_structure: A single unbroken free-verse lyric of visionary images, with no stanza divisions and a closing assertion that turns the description into a blessing.
meter_and_prosody: Unpunctuated free verse in a single long sentence; repetition of 'the white bear'; images of ice, ebony, moon and cradle; and an incantatory syntax that holds the poem together without argument.
historical_context: The poem was written in 1983, the year Harjo published She Had Some Horses and finished her MFA, and it belongs to the period in which Native American writers were making ceremonial and mythic material central to their poetics. The bear as a figure of power and of the north is widespread in Native North American traditions, and Harjo uses it without assigning it to a particular nation or story.
literary_significance: 'White Bear' is one of the most anthologised poems in She Had Some Horses and a standard example of the visionary mode in Native American poetry; it is a Norton selection, and with 'Call It Fear' it represents the collection. The Norton list carried it as undated before this wave.
bibliographical_notes: First published in She Had Some Horses (New York: Thunder's Mouth Press, 1983); collected in How We Became Human: New and Selected Poems (New York: W. W. Norton, 2004). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the visionary and the dream, treated as legitimate knowledge rather than as fancy. The second is balance and precariousness, since the poem's world is held in a cradle that could tip. The third is the northern landscape and its animals, which the poem uses as spiritual presences. The fourth is the daughter, who connects the cosmic vision to a family and a future.
summary: The poem begins 'Somewhere, she dreamed, there is the white bear / moving down from the north' and describes the bear motioning its paws 'like a long arctic night'. It holds images of balance - 'the whole world balanced in between', carved of ebony and ice - and of the speaker's daughter's eyes, black nights, and the white bear moon like an ivory cradle. Its closing movement turns on the tipping of that cradle: 'it could go either way', and the poem ends with the assertion that 'all darkness is open to light'.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem's bear as a figure of the sacred without doctrinal content and notes the poem's movement from dream to blessing; the standard accounts of Harjo's early work place it among the poems that establish her association of animal presence, landscape and dream.
research_notes: The 1983 date rests on the collection's publication and on Harjo's own account of writing the poem that year; the text was read from the collection. The Norton list carried the poem as undated before this wave, and this record fixes it.

title: Summer Night
description: 'Summer Night' is in In Mad Love and War (Middletown: Wesleyan University Press, 1990), Harjo's fourth collection and the one that won the American Book Award. It is a short love poem that holds desire and the memory of violence in the same night.
plot_or_argument: The poem's subject is the difficulty of being present with another person when the body remembers injury, and its technique is to keep the two registers in the same sentence. Harjo does not separate the love poem from the history of violence against women; the summer night's heat is both erotic and oppressive, and the insects' noise is both the sound of the world and a kind of vigilance. The poem's tenderness is not naive - it is a decision made in full knowledge - and that is what distinguishes In Mad Love and War, whose title announces the book's two subjects. The line is longer here than in She Had Some Horses, and the poem's rhythm is more conversational, which belongs to the widening of Harjo's style in the late 1980s, when she began writing poems that could carry political statement without losing their lyric intensity.
narrative_structure: A short free-verse lyric in a single movement, built on the alternation of sensory description and intimate address, ending on a turn toward the present.
meter_and_prosody: Conversational free verse with longer lines than the earlier books; sensory and nocturnal imagery; direct address to a lover; and a refusal of rhetorical closure.
historical_context: In Mad Love and War was published by Wesleyan in 1990 and won the American Book Award; it belongs to the years in which Harjo was teaching in New Mexico and Arizona and performing with her band, and its poems move between the Southwest, Oklahoma and the wider world. It is the middle book between She Had Some Horses (1983) and The Woman Who Fell from the Sky (1994).
literary_significance: The poem is a standard selection from In Mad Love and War and represents the erotic and conversational side of Harjo's work in the anthology, which otherwise draws on her visionary and political poems. It is a Norton selection.
bibliographical_notes: First published in In Mad Love and War (Middletown, CT: Wesleyan University Press, 1990); collected in How We Became Human (2004). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is love and desire, treated as an act of will in difficult conditions. The second is the memory of violence, which is present in the poem without being narrated. The third is the natural world as a witness and a participant. The fourth is the present moment, which the poem claims as the ground of any possible happiness.
summary: The poem places two people together on a summer night, in a landscape of heat and insects, and it moves between the immediacy of touch and the knowledge that the past is still present in the body. Its images are of the natural world at night - the sound of insects, the dark, the warmth - and its address is intimate. It closes on a statement of the present as the only place love can happen, held against what has happened before.
critical_context: Criticism reads the collection's love poems as continuous with its political ones, and the standard account of Harjo's development treats In Mad Love and War as the book in which she widened her line and admitted a more directly personal voice.
research_notes: The poem's first periodical appearance was not established; the 1990 collection date is the earliest publication found.

title: The Flood
description: 'The Flood' is in The Woman Who Fell from the Sky (New York: W. W. Norton, 1994), the collection Harjo published the year after she began teaching at the University of Tucson. It is a narrative poem about water, loss and the return of what has been buried.
plot_or_argument: 'The Flood' is characteristic of the collection in which Harjo turned from the short visionary lyric to poems with more narrative reach; its subject is not only a weather event but the way catastrophe rearranges a life and exposes what a community has been carrying. Water in Harjo's work is never only literal: it is the element that crosses boundaries, carries the dead and refuses to respect the divisions between past and present. The poem's narrative is episodic and its syntax is closer to speech than in the earlier books, and its power comes from the flatness with which terrible things are reported - the tone is not hysterical, and that calm is what makes it frightening. The collection's title, the Seneca story of the woman who fell from the sky onto the back of a turtle, is the mythic frame behind the poem, and 'The Flood' is one of the pieces in which the frame becomes visible: the world is remade after the water, and what survives is carried by the women who remember.
narrative_structure: A free-verse narrative in stanzas of varying length, moving chronologically through the flood and its aftermath, with interruptions of remembered speech and no formal climax.
meter_and_prosody: Conversational free verse with narrative momentum; concrete images of water, mud and damaged objects; a flat, unhurried report tone; and a refusal of metaphor at the moments of greatest loss.
historical_context: The Woman Who Fell from the Sky appeared from Norton in 1994; it was Harjo's first book with a major New York publisher and followed her move to teaching in Arizona and her work with the Native American poetry community. The collection's title myth is Iroquoian, and its use by a Muscogee poet is part of the pan-tribal character of the Native American Renaissance.
literary_significance: The poem is a selected example of Harjo's narrative mode and represents the 1994 collection in the Norton; with the three earlier poems it gives the anthology a twenty-year span of her work, which is unusual for any poet in the period.
bibliographical_notes: First published in The Woman Who Fell from the Sky (New York: W. W. Norton, 1994); collected in How We Became Human (2004). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is catastrophe and its aftermath, natural and historical at once. The second is the survival of Indigenous people and the memory of removal, carried in the image of water that has taken land. The third is memory, since the flood releases what was buried. The fourth is the mythic frame of the collection, which turns a weather event into a story of the world's remaking.
summary: The poem tells of a flood that rises and takes what is in its path, and it moves between the physical event and the memories the water releases. Its images are of water carrying possessions, animals and the dead, and of survivors afterwards in the mud. The poem's voice is a witness's, and its movement is from catastrophe through loss to a settled knowledge of what has been changed.
critical_context: Criticism reads The Woman Who Fell from the Sky as the book in which Harjo's mythic frame became explicit and her line became more narrative; the standard account of the collection treats the falling-woman story as its organising figure, and the flood poems as its earthly instances.
research_notes: The poem's first periodical appearance was not established; the 1994 collection date is the earliest publication found.
